newsitem.title: UK: European stocks show no signs of losing steam.
newsitem.headline: European stocks show no signs of losing steam.

text.p: As another Wall Street record sent leading European bourses to new peaks on Tuesday, market experts forecast more gains as long as a "dream combination" of steady growth and low inflation lasts.

Buoyed by the latest advance in U.S. markets, where the Dow Jones industrial average closed above 6,000 for the first time on Monday, leading share indices in Britain and Germany set new highs, while France's CAC-40 index rose to its highest level since May 1994.

Although any early hint of resurgent inflation could still derail the rally, pundits said investors were likely to pump more cash into European equities as prospects for profit and dividend growth in 1997 improve.
"The economic background is about as good as it gets," said Peter Sullivan, European equity strategist at U.S. investment bank Goldman Sachs in London.
"We are looking for a strong rebound in growth in Europe in 1997 but interest rates are still set to fall. That's a combination that happens only about once a decade."

European markets marked time at best for much of the summer on growing fears that the pace of growth in the U.S. economy was fast enough to prompt the Federal Reserve to raise U.S. interest rates -- which set a benchmark for rates around the world.
Higher rates are bad news for shares since they threaten to curb profit growth while luring investment funds out of stock markets and into the relative safety of bank deposits.
And with Wall Street already having risen strongly since the start of 1995 -- when the Dow was below 4,000 -- there were fears that any rise in U.S. rates could bring the bull run to a sudden end.
Memories of the crash of 1987, nine years ago this month, are never far from investors' and traders' minds.
Yet European stock markets sprang to life in recent weeks as signs of a slowdown in the U.S. economy raised hopes that any increase in U.S. rates could be put off until next year.
And with U.S. rates on hold, the way was cleared for Germany's Bundesbank to lead another round of rate reductions across Europe.
"One of the markets' fears was that if the Fed moved, markets would crack," said Gary Dugan, European strategist at U.S. investment bank J.P. Morgan.

"But any Fed move has probably been put off to next year and that has given room for the markets to move higher," Dugan said. "Generally we are still getting good news on inflation and there is a gentle pick up in growth. That's positive for equities."
In Britain, too, the chances of a rate increase this year have dwindled as the recent strength of sterling bears down on the price of imports, helping keep a lid on price pressures.
Meanwhile, European markets could have further to run as prospects improve for European growth in 1997 -- promising a boost to profit and dividend growth even if bond markets run out of steam.
"I think we will see some positive earnings surprises in 1997," said Sullivan at Goldman.

Strategists said the benign economic environment in Europe could carry through at least until the middle of next year -- though the rally could boil over on any unexpected signal that growth was overheating and the next move in rates would be up.
As usual, the most immediate risk to markets comes from the United States, where any sign of a rebound in economic growth could rekindle the inflation worries that have abated in recent months.
Said Dugan at J.P. Morgan: "The risk is still that if we get one bad number out of the U.S., that could reverse everything."
